title: How to use this course

story: You open the course for the first time. There is a map with nine islands, and behind them are 140 lessons and the 242 tickets of our AI-agent platform. You have about forty minutes tonight. The obvious plan is to start at lesson one, play every video, read every page in order, and keep going until the end, the way you would watch a series.

That plan feels productive, and it works badly. Two weeks later you open a real platform ticket that asks you to write a small service, and you recognise every word in it, but you cannot start, because so far you only watched other people do things. Recognising is not the same as being able to do it.
hook.question: How do I use this course so that, at the end, I can actually do the tickets and not only recognise the words?

read.h: The map is one ticket's journey
p: The course opens on a map (its address ends in #/islands). Each island is one stop on the road a ticket travels through our platform. Work arrives at the Ticket Dock, where someone assigns a Jira ticket to an agent. The Clock Tower is Temporal, the engine that runs every job and remembers where it is. The Machine Harbor and the Sandbox are where a fresh machine is prepared and where the agent works. The Model Gate and the Key Vault guard the doors to Claude, GitHub and Jira. The Review Observatory is where a pull request is reviewed and approved, and the Lighthouse is where we measure everything. A ninth island, the Fix-it Workshop, holds the agents that repair things on their own, such as a broken main branch.

Press Tour the platform once, at the top of the map. It moves one example ticket, RH-1234, across the islands in eight stops. That ticket asks for a small "No projects yet" card in the product, and you will meet it in almost every lesson, because one familiar example makes every new idea easier to place.

Click an island and a panel opens beside the map: what the island is, and its lessons in order. A lesson marked ready to play is rebuilt in the format described here; the others say Coming soon, because the course is being rebuilt island by island. On the left of the map, Your path lists every ready lesson in course order and names the next one, so on a tired evening you do not have to decide where to go.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the three kinds of parts behind the map
p: The lessons belong to 22 parts. This part, Start here, is four lessons of orientation. Thirteen foundation parts teach one tool each, the tools the platform is built with: Node services, GitHub Apps and Actions, AWS, Terraform, Kubernetes, telemetry, Temporal, the Claude Agent SDK, Slack and Jira from code, Python, the security walls, and skills and evals.

Nine walkthrough parts follow the nine goals of the plan and teach the tickets themselves. The Classic view link at the top of the map opens the older layout, which has a ticket map: all 242 tickets, the lesson that teaches each one, and a counter of how many you can already do.

A lesson opens as a sheet with six steps along the top: Story, Watch, Understand, Practice, Build and Checkpoint. They are listed in a sensible order, but each one stands on its own, so you can jump straight to Build if you learn best with your hands, or open the Checkpoint first to find out whether you already know the topic. A tick appears on every step you have opened.

The steps do two different jobs. Watch and Understand put the idea into your head: Watch has two to four clips from real YouTube videos, each starting and stopping on the minutes that matter, and Understand explains the idea with real code and real output. Practice, Build and Checkpoint make you take the idea out again: you answer drills, you build something on your laptop, you answer three questions. The second kind feels harder and slower, and it is the kind that makes the idea stay. Pulling something out of memory changes the memory itself, which is why a short test teaches more than another reading. The clips of this lesson show the research behind that.

So guess before you know. Every drill, every lab and every Checkpoint asks you to commit to an answer first. A wrong guess is cheap here, and a guess that proves wrong makes the right answer much easier to remember afterwards.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what is inside each step
p: Story is a short scene with a problem you can feel, ending with the question the lesson answers. Watch shows each clip with why it is there, two or three things to watch for, and how it connects to our platform; you can mark a clip as watched. Understand ends with two cards: Words, the new terms in plain language, and In our platform, which says where the idea lives in our plan and which tickets it unlocks. That card is the only place where ticket keys appear.

Practice has quick drills: choose an answer, fill a blank in real code, or put steps in order, and some lessons add a small simulator you can break on purpose. Checkpoint has three questions about the one idea of the lesson, a Remember line, and a few tasks to come back to later.

Every lab runs on your laptop with free tools, in a folder of its own. No lab touches a company system, uses company credentials or costs money; where the real thing needs the cloud, the lab uses a local copy or a dry run. There are two kinds of lab.

A checked lab is a small project with one piece missing. You start it from the course folder with ./academy lab followed by the lesson id. That copies the starter code into ~/academy-labs/<id>, installs its packages and prints the steps. You write the missing piece, and ./academy check runs the lab's checks on your code and prints one line per check: ✔ when it holds, ✘ with the reason when it does not. A ✘ on a fresh lab is normal: it is the lab telling you what to write first. When every check passes, it prints a pass code that you paste on the lesson page, and the lab is marked as passed.

A guided lab has the same five parts (Guess, Follow along, Build it, Fix it, Explain it) but no checker. You run real commands and compare your output with the output on the page, and Build it ends with a short checklist that you tick yourself, with one possible solution behind Stuck?. When the whole list is true for you, press I finished this lab. This lesson's lab is a guided one.
In both kinds, when your output is different from the page, stop and find out why before you continue. Most of what a lab teaches is in those differences.

code.text:
./academy lab p0-2      # copy the lab into ~/academy-labs/p0-2 and print its steps
cd ~/academy-labs/p0-2
./academy check         # one line per check: ✔ or ✘ with the reason
./academy hint          # one hint; run it again for a bigger one

notes.text: The lab id is the lesson id. If the folder already exists, your work is kept; add --fresh to start again from the starter code.
Exit code 0 when everything passes (then it prints the pass code), 1 when something is still missing.
Hints come one at a time, from a small nudge to almost the answer. The tool remembers how many you have seen.

read.see:
Checking your build for p0-2 (Follow one ticket) in ~/academy-labs/p0-2

✘ canMerge is not written yet: approval.mjs still throws the TODO error, so replace that line with the three rules
  · 10 more checks wait until this one passes

→ stuck? ./academy hint

p: ./academy check --fix runs the same checks on the Fix it folder, where a teammate's code is broken on purpose. ./academy diff shows your file next to the lab's solution, which is useful after you pass, to compare two ways of writing the same thing. ./academy explain asks the three Explain it questions in the terminal, saves your answers in ~/academy-labs/notes, and prints a prompt you can paste into Claude to find what you missed.

Every command works from the course folder and from inside a lab folder, because each lab folder gets a small academy link back to the course. After the first ./academy lab, the id is optional: the tool uses the lab folder you are in, or else the last lab you started.

read.h: Mark it done, and come back later
p: There is no automatic finish line. When you feel that you own the idea of a lesson, press Mark as done at the top right of the lesson; the lesson gets a tick on Your path and its island grows a little brighter. You decide, because only you know whether you could explain the idea to a teammate without the page open.

Your progress (lessons done, answers, labs passed, clips watched) is saved only in this browser, in its local storage, which is a small store each website keeps on your machine. Another browser, another laptop or clearing the site's data starts you from zero, so use one browser for the course.

Each Checkpoint ends with Come back to these in a few days: two or three small tasks, such as writing three lines of code from memory. Do them two or three days later, before you look at the lesson again. Remembering after a gap feels harder than rereading, and that effort is exactly what makes the idea last.

Almost every lab needs four things: Node 22 or newer, git, Docker with its engine running, and the course folder. The course itself is a small React app that runs on your laptop, so you can also read it offline. The platform we build runs on Node 24, so if you install a new Node today, choose 24.

Some parts need one more tool, and each lab lists it under what it needs: the temporal command line for the Temporal part, OpenTofu for the infrastructure parts, Python 3 for the Python part. Install each one when a lab asks for it, not today. Everything here is free.

code.text:
node --version                                # v22 or newer
git --version
docker info --format '{{.ServerVersion}}'     # the Docker engine must be running
git clone https://github.com/seanazu/agent-platform-academy.git ~/Projects/ai-agents-course
cd ~/Projects/ai-agents-course && npm install
npm run dev                                   # then open http://localhost:4310/#/islands

notes.text: An older Node is the most common reason a lab fails in a confusing way. With nvm: nvm install 24, then nvm use 24.
Prints the engine version. An error such as "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon" means Docker Desktop is not running yet.
Skip this line if you already have the course folder. The folder name is up to you; the labs only need ./academy from inside it.
Leave this terminal open while you use the course. Ctrl+C stops it.

lab.title: Prepare your laptop and meet your first check
lab.goal: Check your tools, run the course on your laptop, and start one checked lab far enough to see its first ✘ line and its first hint.

guess.q: You start a checked lab and run ./academy check at once, before you write any code. What does it print?

options.text: Nothing, because there is no code of yours to check yet.
options.why: The checks run on the starter code, which is already in your folder. They always have something to say.

options.text: One or more ✘ lines that say what is missing, and it exits with code 1.
options.why: A fresh lab fails on purpose. The first ✘ line is the lab telling you what to write first.

options.text: An error saying the lab is broken and must be installed again.
options.why: A failing check is not a broken lab. Starting again with --fresh would only bring back the same ✘.

follow.say: Check Node first, because a Node that is too old is the most common reason a lab fails in a confusing way. Any version from 22 up is fine.
Check git and Docker, because many labs use both. Docker must be running, not only installed.
Get the course folder and install its packages. If you already have the folder, only run the second line.

lab.build: Now find a lab on your own, using only the map. Open the Fix-it Workshop island, open the lesson One red main, one fixer, and go to its Build step to read the lab's id. Start that lab from the terminal, run the first command of its Follow along list, then run ./academy check. Write down the first ✘ line in your own words: what does it want you to write? Ask for one hint and check that it points at the same thing. Do not solve the lab; that is that lesson's work.
checks: node --version prints v22 or higher, and docker info prints a version number instead of an error.
http://localhost:4310/#/islands shows the map with nine islands, and Your path names a next lesson.
~/academy-labs/p0-2 exists and contains approval.mjs, journey.mjs and an academy link.
In ~/academy-labs/p0-2, ./academy check prints a ✘ line about canMerge and the exit code is 1.
You started the Fix-it Workshop lab from the map alone, and you can say in one sentence what its first ✘ line asks for.

solution.file: one way to do the Build step
solution.text:
# On the map: Fix-it Workshop → One red main, one fixer → Build. The lab id is g5-2.
cd ~/Projects/ai-agents-course && ./academy lab g5-2
cd ~/academy-labs/g5-2 && node storm.mjs
#   7 red builds on main → 7 fixer runs  a storm of fixers
./academy check
#   ✘ firstError is not written yet: fingerprint.mjs still throws the TODO error there
# In my words: write firstError(log), which finds the first error line in a build log.
./academy hint
#   Hint 1 of 4: compare two FAIL lines and write down every part that is different.

lab.fix: A teammate opens a new terminal, types ./academy lab p0-2 and gets zsh: no such file or directory: ./academy. Their Node is fine and the course folder exists. Find out which folder their terminal is in, and name the two kinds of folder where ./academy works.
explain: Which three steps of a lesson make you produce something, and why do they teach more than reading the same page again?
What does a ✘ line on a fresh checked lab mean, and what do you do next?
Where is your progress saved, and what would make it disappear?
lab.done: Your tools print their versions, the map runs on localhost:4310, and you can explain the first ✘ line of a lab you found on your own.

check.q: You have 30 minutes left tonight and you are tired. Which use of them helps you most next week?

options.text: Watch all the clips of three lessons, because watching is the fastest way to get through a lot of material.
options.why: You would see a lot and keep little. Watching only puts ideas in; nothing makes you take them out again.

options.text: Open one lesson, guess the answers to its Practice drills before reading, then read Understand to see what you got wrong.
options.why: Guessing first and checking afterwards is retrieval. Even the wrong guesses make the explanation stick.

options.text: Read the Understand step of one lesson three times, until it feels familiar.
options.why: Familiar is the trap: rereading feels like progress, but you cannot tell whether you could do it without the page.

check.q: You start a lab and ./academy check prints "✘ firstError is not written yet". What does it mean?

options.text: It is the normal start: the checker is telling you which piece to write first.
options.why: A fresh checked lab fails on purpose. Each ✘ names what is missing and why, and ./academy hint helps if the line is not enough.

options.text: The lab did not install correctly, so you should start it again with --fresh.
options.why: --fresh copies the same starter code again, so you would see the same ✘. Nothing is broken.

options.text: Your Node version is too old for the lab.
options.why: An old Node gives a loading or syntax error before any check runs. A ✘ line means the checks did run.

check.q: A lesson's Build step shows commands, expected output and a checklist, but no ./academy command. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it until the lab gets a checker, because a lab without one cannot tell you whether you passed.
options.why: You can tell: the checklist lists what must be true. The learning is in running the commands, not in the checker.

options.text: Read the commands and their output carefully instead of running them, since nothing checks you.
options.why: Reading output is like watching a video. You learn from typing the commands and seeing your own output differ.

options.text: It is a guided lab: run the commands, compare your output, do Build it, tick the checklist, then press I finished this lab.
options.why: A guided lab has the same five parts as a checked one. You are the checker, with the list and the solution behind Stuck? to help.

p: The course follows the plan for our AI-agent platform: one walkthrough part for each of its nine goals, so the parts called G0 to G8 match the goals with the same names. Each of the 242 tickets is taught by exactly one walkthrough lesson, and the foundation lessons teach the tools those tickets use.
This lesson unlocks no ticket by itself. The next lesson follows RH-1234 through the whole platform, and the two after it show the order the plan is built in and the repos the work lands in.

words.plain: One stop on a ticket's journey through the platform. Each island on the map holds the lessons about that stop.
The list on the left of the map with every ready lesson in course order and the next one to do.
A lab with a small project and a checker: ./academy check prints ✔ or ✘ per check and a pass code at the end.
A lab with real commands, the output you should see and a checklist that you tick yourself.
The code ./academy check prints when every check passes; pasting it on the lesson page marks the lab passed.
A small store each website keeps in your browser. The course saves your progress there, and only there.

review.q: From memory, name the six steps of a lesson and say which three make you produce something.
review.a: Story, Watch, Understand, Practice, Build, Checkpoint. Practice, Build and Checkpoint make you produce answers or code, and that retrieval is what makes an idea stay.

review.q: Without looking, write the three commands that start a checked lab, check it and ask for a hint.
review.a: ./academy lab <id> from the course folder, then ./academy check and ./academy hint (from the course folder or the lab folder).

review.q: A friend wants to continue the course on their home laptop where they left off at work. What do you tell them?
review.a: Progress lives in the browser's local storage on the work laptop, so the home laptop starts from zero. Use one browser for the course.

remember: Open the steps in any order, but always do the ones that make you produce something: guess, practise, build, and come back a few days later.
